title: The mental hospital he designed took him in with dementia; at the end, he still griped it wasn't built to his plan
dek: He personally designed the grounds of McLean Hospital; 26 years later he moved there with dementia, and still recognized that the building wasn't constructed according to his plan.
why: This is the second half of a two-part series with information density no less than the first episode: the Civil War Sanitary Commission, gold mine strikes, the Yosemite report, Riverside suburb planning—all leading to him entering the mental hospital he had designed decades earlier.
who: Readers interested in urban planning, the history of park design, or post-Civil War American social reconstruction, and anyone wanting to understand the later life of Central Park's designer.
skip: The reader-mail section at the end—black cat photos and book recommendations—is unrelated to Olmsted's story in this episode and can be skipped.

points.h: During the Civil War, he saved lives before designing parks
points.body: After leaving Central Park, Olmsted was injured in a carriage accident and unfit to enlist. He was appointed executive secretary of the American Sanitary Commission—the precursor to the American Red Cross. The commission inspected camp sanitation, coordinated medical supplies, and operated hospital ships. By his estimate, he helped treat nearly 8,000 wounded and sick soldiers over the course of the war. But his work style was as extreme as during the Central Park years: friend George Templeton Strong recorded in his diary that Olmsted would disappear for days at a time, sleeping only after four in the morning, and living on strong coffee and pickles for breakfast.

points.h: He tried to design a system for freed Black people and lost
points.body: Olmsted was deeply involved in relief for escaped or captured Black people (called contrabands at the time), and once sought the position of contraband commissioner. After federal occupation of South Carolina's Sea Islands, he drafted a plan proposing paid labor for the freed to continue cotton cultivation while receiving education and training. He naively believed this would demonstrate to the South that slavery was an ‘economic mistake’. Through Senator Foster, the proposal passed the Senate but was rejected in the House. Eventually another man, E.L. Pierce, led what became known as the ‘Port Royal Experiment’.

points.h: He solved the gold mine owner's error by cutting workers' wages
points.body: When Olmsted took over managing the Mariposa Gold Mine in California, his predecessor had worked only the easily accessible ore veins, leaving harder sections undeveloped and the company cash-depleted. Olmsted's remedy was wage cuts, hiring less-skilled but cheaper workers, and after a strike, introducing Chinese laborers as replacements—which angered existing workers and fueled anti-Chinese sentiment. Though a federal investigation later cleared him of misconduct, it called the entire affair ‘absurd stupidity’. The mine verged on bankruptcy after he departed, but he used the salary and shrewd investment to finally clear years of personal debt.

points.h: He wrote a report arguing parks are a political duty; it vanished
points.body: In 1864, Lincoln set aside Yosemite Valley for California—the federal government's first time explicitly reserving land for public recreation. Olmsted was tasked with writing a report requesting $37,000 for roads, cottages, and surveying, arguing that natural beauty had previously been a monopoly of the wealthy few, and that government had a political duty to make it accessible to all. But the report was never formally submitted to California or federal authorities, and the proposal went nowhere. It wasn't until 1952 that biographer Laura Wood Roper rediscovered and published it—though its arguments are now recognized as foreshadowing Yellowstone and the entire national park system.

points.h: He mistook indigenous ecological wisdom for destructive behavior
points.body: Olmsted was entirely unaware that indigenous people had been managing Yosemite Valley for generations. Instead he saw them as ‘obstacles’ to be removed so the land could be ‘enjoyed by all’. In his report, he described the indigenous practice of forest burning as harmful behavior, without recognizing that this very cultural practice had created the meadow beauty he praised elsewhere in the same document.

points.h: America's first planned suburb and park system both came from him
points.body: In 1868, he and Vaux designed Riverside outside Chicago, the country's first planned suburb, with curved roads and private lots meant to ease the strain of urban life. High construction costs bankrupted the developer after the Chicago Fire and the 1873 Panic. Starting that same year, they designed America's first coordinated park system in Buffalo, New York—three parks connected by landscaped ‘parkways’, which pioneered a concept that would reshape American urban design.

points.h: The mental hospital he designed admitted him as his mind failed
points.body: Beginning in 1895, Olmsted's memory declined and he gradually transferred his work to stepson John Charles and son Rick. That same year, Vaux drowned during a morning walk in Brooklyn. His wife Mary feared the news would kill him, so she kept it secret for a full year. In 1898, unable to care for him alone, the 68-year-old Mary admitted him to McLean Hospital in Belmont, Massachusetts—the same institution whose grounds Olmsted himself had personally selected and designed in 1872. On arrival he still recognized his handiwork and said, ‘They didn't build it according to my plan—damn them.’
